lead: A proximity sensor answers: is the target here yet? It turns a short-range physical change — metal near a coil, or any object near an electrode — into a clean ON/OFF signal. Nothing touches the target, so nothing wears. Factories use them to count parts, find the end of a press stroke, guard a gate, and sense liquid level through a tank wall. Some syllabi call them proximity switches, because the output is a switch, not a measurement.
prereq: You need: 3.4 Eddy current transducers for why a conductor near a coil changes its impedance, and the threshold and calibration ideas from the static characteristics of sensors.

blocks.text: One sensor cannot switch at the same distance for every target, so the datasheet fixes the target, temperature and supply voltage first.

Rated sensing distance Sn is the switching distance with a standard square mild-steel target at 20–25 °C and rated supply voltage. It compares sensors; it is not a promise for your part. With that target the real operate point can fall between 0.9 Sn and 1.1 Sn.

blocks.where: S is usable switching distance in mm for the actual target; K is the material correction factor from the datasheet, 1.00 for mild steel; S<sub>n</sub> is rated sensing distance in mm. K values differ by maker.

blocks.text: Hysteresis is the gap between ON distance as the target approaches and OFF distance as it leaves; release is farther. It stops chattering when a part rests at the field edge. Repeatability is the spread of the operate point over repeated cycles, usually a few percent of Sn.

Flush (shielded) sensors have a metal ring round the coil, so the field leaves only from the front face; they can sit in a steel bracket. Non-flush (unshielded) types reach farther but need clear space round the face.
The sensing element is a coil on a ferrite core behind the face, driven by an oscillator at roughly 100 kHz to 1 MHz.

items: The oscillator holds the coil at fixed frequency and steady amplitude in air.
A metal target enters the field. Alternating flux induces eddy currents in it (see 3.4).
Eddy currents dissipate energy as heat. The energy comes from the coil, so field amplitude falls.
A peak detector rectifies coil voltage and feeds a Schmitt trigger, a comparator with two thresholds. These are the datasheet hysteresis.
Below the lower threshold the output turns ON; above the upper threshold, as the target leaves, it turns OFF.

blocks.text: Iron and steel are magnetic and conductive, so they change inductance too and give the longest range. Aluminium, copper and brass only carry eddy currents, lose less energy, and need K below 1.

The output is a transistor switch, not a relay contact. A PNP (sourcing) output connects the load to +24 V when ON; an NPN (sinking) output connects it to 0 V. Normally open (NO) conducts only with a target present; normally closed (NC) conducts until a target appears, the safe choice for a guard.

sections.h3: Capacitive: the target changes a capacitor

blocks.text: A capacitive sensor uses a flat metal electrode behind the face as one capacitor plate. The target is the other plate, and the gap is the dielectric.

blocks.where: C is capacitance in farads; ε₀ = 8.85 × 10<sup>−12</sup> F/m; ε<sub>r</sub> is relative permittivity of the gap material (about 1 for air, 80 for water); A is effective plate area in m²; d is gap in m.

blocks.text: A hand, plastic bottle or rising liquid raises ε<sub>r</sub> in the gap, so C rises. The circuit turns C into a voltage — often an RC oscillator whose frequency falls as C rises — and a threshold stage switches the output.

It detects paper, plastic, wood, grain and water, and senses level through a plastic tank wall without touching the liquid. Drift is the weakness: humidity, dust and condensation on the face change C too, so most units carry a sensitivity trimmer. Range depends on ε<sub>r</sub>, so water switches from far away while thin plastic must come closer.

items: Counting parts. A sensor over a conveyor gives one pulse per part; a counter or PLC adds them up.
End of stroke. On a hydraulic press, a sensor on the frame confirms the ram has reached the bottom before the next step.
Safety guard. An NC sensor on a gate holds a safety relay closed; when the gate opens, the machine stops.
Level. A capacitive sensor clamped outside a plastic tank switches when the liquid inside reaches its height.
Speed. Counting pulses from a rotating gear's teeth in one second and dividing by the number of teeth gives revolutions per second: pulses per second ÷ number of teeth.

Hospital equipment. Lid and door interlocks on centrifuges and sterilisers, bed and table position limits, and capacitive sensors that detect an empty infusion bottle or a reservoir level through the plastic wall.

figure.caption: Worked example 1 drawn to scale. Each metal switches at S = K·S<sub>n</sub>, but only within 0.9 S is it certain; the brass target at 5.2 mm and the stainless one at 7.3 mm both sit in the uncertain band. Worked example 2 reads a centrifuge: 400 pulses per second from 4 slots is 6000 rev/min.

examples.question: An inductive sensor has S<sub>n</sub> = 10 mm for mild steel. Datasheet K = 0.50 for brass and 0.70 for stainless steel. (a) A brass target is 5.2 mm away. Is switching guaranteed? (b) What is the maximum brass distance? (c) A stainless-steel target is 7.3 mm away. Is switching guaranteed?
steps: S<sub>n</sub> = 10 mm applies to mild steel, K = 1.00. Other metals scale by K.
Brass: S<sub>brass</sub> = K × S<sub>n</sub> = 0.50 × 10 mm = 5.0 mm.
Brass at 5.2 mm is beyond 5.0 mm. Operate point can reach 1.1 × 5.0 = 5.5 mm, so detection is not guaranteed; reliable only inside 0.9 × 5.0 = 4.5 mm.
Stainless at 7.3 mm is beyond 7.0 mm. Operate point can reach 1.1 × 7.0 = 7.7 mm, so not guaranteed; reliable only inside 0.9 × 7.0 = 6.3 mm.
Both targets are in the uncertain band beyond corrected distance: may switch, but not reliably.
examples.answer: Brass at 5.2 mm against S<sub>brass</sub> = 5.0 mm: not guaranteed; reliable only inside 4.5 mm. Stainless steel at 7.3 mm against S<sub>ss</sub> = 7.0 mm: not guaranteed; reliable only inside 6.3 mm.

examples.question: A clinical centrifuge’s speed is read by an inductive sensor facing a steel disc with 4 slots. (a) The sensor gives 400 pulses per second: find the speed in rev/min. (b) The top speed is 15 000 rev/min: can a sensor rated for 800 Hz switching frequency follow it?
steps: Each revolution gives 4 pulses, so rev/s = pulses per second ÷ 4 = 400/4 = 100 rev/s.
At 15 000 rev/min: 15 000/60 = 250 rev/s, so pulse rate = 250 × 4 = 1000 Hz.
1000 Hz exceeds the 800 Hz rating: pulses would be missed and the reading would be low at top speed.
Choose a sensor rated at least 1.5 kHz (50 % margin), or a disc with fewer slots: 2 slots give 500 Hz at top speed.
examples.answer: 6000 rev/min; at 15 000 rev/min the pulse rate is 1000 Hz, beyond the 800 Hz sensor, so a faster sensor (≥ 1.5 kHz) or fewer slots is needed.

traps: Using S<sub>n</sub> for every metal. S<sub>n</sub> is for standard mild steel; other materials need S = K × S<sub>n</sub>, with K below 1 for brass, aluminium and copper.
Ignoring hysteresis. Release distance is larger than operate point, so a target that just switched ON may not switch OFF when it moves back by the same small amount.

Confusing flush and non-flush. A shielded sensor can sit flush in steel without losing range because its ring keeps the field at the face. An unshielded sensor reaches farther but needs free space around the face; metal beside it changes the field.
Swapping NPN and PNP. A sinking input expects a sourcing (PNP) sensor; the wrong pair gives no signal or a short through the output transistor.
Calling capacitive type a distance meter. It is a switch, and range depends strongly on ε<sub>r</sub>, so water switches from far away while thin plastic must come closer.

quiz.q: Define rated sensing distance S<sub>n</sub> of an inductive proximity sensor.
quiz.a: Switching distance measured with a standard mild-steel target at 20–25 °C and rated supply voltage. It compares sensors, not predicts other metals.

quiz.q: Why is release distance larger than operate distance, and what does that buy the user?
quiz.a: The threshold circuit is a Schmitt trigger with two levels. Output turns ON below the lower amplitude and OFF only after amplitude recovers above the upper level. This hysteresis stops chattering when a part rests at the field edge.

quiz.q: A sensor has S<sub>n</sub> = 12 mm and K = 0.45 for aluminium. An aluminium target sits 5.0 mm away. Is it detected, and what is the maximum aluminium distance?
quiz.a: S = K × S<sub>n</sub> = 0.45 × 12 mm = 5.4 mm. Target at 5.0 mm is inside 5.4 mm, so detected. Maximum is 5.4 mm; guaranteed switching within 0.9 × 5.4 = 4.86 mm.

quiz.q: An inductive sensor counts steel parts correctly but misses aluminium parts of the same size at the same gap. Explain and suggest two fixes.
quiz.a: Aluminium gives weaker eddy currents and no magnetic inductance change, so field loss at that gap stays above threshold. Fixes: choose a larger S<sub>n</sub> sensor, reduce gap to stay inside K × S<sub>n</sub>, or use a capacitive sensor that responds to any metal at short range.

quiz.q: A machine guard uses a normally-open PNP sensor wired to a sinking PLC input. The machine keeps running even when the gate is open. Give likely causes and the fix.
quiz.a: With an NO sensor the PLC input is ON only while the target is present, so the program reads ON as guard closed. A shorted cable, stuck-ON output transistor or inverted program leaves input permanently ON. A broken wire gives the opposite symptom. Check input LED, then confirm PNP sensor on sinking input. For fail-safe use an NC sensor on matching input, so any fault or break de-energises the safety relay and stops the machine.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern inductive sensors add IO-Link, a digital link reporting actual distance and switching counts. Search for IEC 60947-5-2 on sensing distances and “capacitive level sensor dielectric constant”.
